body.text: Drive north from Tel Aviv towards the Galilee another Israel gradually comes into view. Arabic becomes more prominent on shopfronts and signboards. Nazareth, the largest Arab city in northern Israel, sits amid a constellation of Arab towns and villages.

Sakhnin, Arraba, Kafr Manda, Shefa-Amr, and Tamra are spread across the hills and plains of the north. Farther south lies the Triangle, a chain of predominantly Arab towns near the Green Line, including Umm al-Fahm, Tayibe, and Tira. In the Negev, large Bedouin communities live in and around Rahat and in villages, some of which the Israeli state does not recognise.

Across these towns and villages, on October 1, almost everybody was glued to television and phone screens watching the proceedings of Israel’s Supreme Court in West Jerusalem, where a case of unusual consequence for the country’s Arab citizens was being heard. At stake was not simply the fate of a few candidates, but whether the principal political formations representing a community of more than two million people will be allowed to contest the October 27 election.

Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously overturned the Central Elections Committee’s decision to bar the Arab-majority Joint List from running in the upcoming election. Convening in its capacity as the High Court of Justice—which directly reviews state and regulatory decisions—the justices also struck down a ban on the Arab Islamist party Ra’am. Arab parties will now run in the elections.

The Central Elections Committee had disqualified the two principal Arab political formations, the Joint List and Ra’am, or United Arab List. It also barred Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif and former parliamentarian and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. The Supreme Court convened an expanded nine-judge bench to hear the challenges. Israel’s attorney general opposed the disqualification of the two lists, saying the evidence did not meet the stringent legal threshold required to exclude them. While Cassif has been allowed to contest, Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy when it became clear that the court would not approve it.

Outside the court, Arab lawmakers and their supporters demonstrated as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir arrived in a lawyer’s robe to argue for the exclusion of Abu Shehadeh. Cassif, a Jewish member of the predominantly Arab Joint List, told protesters they would fight for “all our children, Palestinians and Israelis, Jews and Arabs”.

Days earlier, Cassif had spelt out the electoral stakes even more trenchantly, describing the Palestinian vote as a possible “game changer”. It is a striking description of a community whose political weight has rarely matched its demographic strength.

Palestinian Arabs constitute roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population. Yet their political parties generally command only around half the number of seats that simple demographic arithmetic might suggest. For a South Asian reader, the paradox has a familiar ring.

For decades, Indian Muslims were described, often too simplistically, as a “vote bank”. In closely contested constituencies in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala, and elsewhere, Muslim voters could help decide which candidate won. Yet only 24 Muslims entered the 543-member Lok Sabha in 2024, around 4.4 per cent of the House, although Muslims accounted for 14.2 per cent of India’s population in the last completed census.

Israel presents almost the reverse electoral architecture. Its Palestinian citizens have distinct political parties, while nationwide proportional representation should make minority votes easier to translate into seats. The problem comes at the next stage: parliamentary representation has not necessarily translated into participation in government.
Between three wars
The map of Arab Israel helps explain how profoundly the wars since October 7, 2023, have affected this community.

The majority of Arab voters live in northern Israel, stretching across the Galilee, the northern valleys, Mount Carmel, and the coastal plain. In the 2022 election, more than 60 per cent of eligible voters in Arab and Druze localities lived in this broader northern region.

In October 2024, a Hezbollah rocket struck the Arab town of Majd al-Krum in Galilee, killing two young residents and wounding seven others. Days later, a mother and son from Shefa-Amr were killed by rocket fire while harvesting olives. A 24-year-old man was killed in Tarshiha, while three people were wounded when rockets struck Tamra.
Alaa Kdah, the assistant mayor of Majd al-Krum, told Frontline over the phone that these attacks exposed inequalities and apartheid that had long troubled Arab municipalities.

“In Majd al-Krum, the shortage of shelters became so serious that the municipality positioned large concrete drainage pipes around the town as makeshift protection. Residents said a town of more than 15,000 people had only around 10 outdoor shelters,” he recalled.

In June 2025, an Iranian ballistic missile struck a three-storey family home in Tamra, about 20 kilometres east of Haifa. Four women from one family were killed: Manar Khatib, her daughters Shada, 20, and Hala, 13, and their relative Manal Khatib. At least 10 others were injured.

Klood Ahmed, a resident of Haifa, said that for Palestinian citizens, the past few years had produced a particularly difficult political and emotional experience. “We watched the devastation of Gaza, whose people share our language, history, and national identity, while we were also running for shelter from Hezbollah rockets and Iranian missiles aimed at Israel,” she said.

The complexities of this identity can perhaps be seen in the journey of Nadine Fahoum, now Nadine Fahoum-Nacar, a Palestinian Arab Muslim from Haifa who was once one of Israel’s most promising young tennis players. She was spoken of as a possible Israeli counterpart to India’s Sania Mirza.

Beginning international competition as a teenager, Fahoum represented Israel in tournaments across more than 30 countries and in 2006 became the first Arab Muslim girl to represent the country at the Youth Olympics.

Yet, wearing Israel’s colours did not insulate her from prejudice. Talking to this writer many years ago, Fahoumrecalledbeing the only Arab child in her Hebrew-language school and hearing anti-Arab remarks during periods of conflict. Most painfully, while travelling to represent Israel at a tournament in Italy, airport security pulled her aside after seeing her Arabic name and subjected her to prolonged questioning even though she was wearing the Israeli flag on her chest. “I was humiliated,” she later said.

Fahoum eventually moved to the US on a tennis scholarship, first attending Old Dominion University and then Duke University, where she became the university’s No. 1 singles player. “I really enjoyed the feeling of not being an Israeli, an Arab, a Muslim. I was just a tennis player,” she told this writer. Her journey from Haifa’s tennis courts to American corporate life offers a revealing glimpse of the competing identities many Palestinian citizens of Israel negotiate.
In the south of Israel, Bedouin citizens were among the victims of the October 7 attack, and Arab citizens were among those who participated in rescue and civilian volunteering.

Their experience does not fit easily into the binaries through which the conflict is often viewed. Palestinian identity connects them profoundly to what has happened in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, while Israeli citizenship places their homes, workplaces, and families inside a country that has itself been attacked. During the past three years, both realities have existed simultaneously.

Surveys capture some of this complexity. Research among Arab citizens after the outbreak of the Gaza war found widespread opposition to the killing and kidnapping of civilians on October 7, alongside growing fear over the consequences of the war and reluctance to speak openly.

By November 2025, a Moshe Dayan Center survey found 74.6 per cent believed relations between Jewish and Arab citizens had deteriorated during the previous two years. Yet 64.6 per cent still supported Arab-Jewish political partnership, while 77.4 per cent favoured an Arab party joining the government after the next election.

A September survey by The Israel Democracy Institute found crime in Arab society was the leading electoral consideration among Arab respondents. Only 32 per cent identified October 7 as central to their voting decision, compared with 68 per cent of Jewish respondents.

These findings help explain the otherwise surprising political appeal of Mansour Abbas, whose argument is that an Arab party should not wait for the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to be resolved before using its parliamentary strength to address crime, housing, planning, education, and municipal budgets.
One country, one constituency

For an Indian accustomed to Amethi, Srinagar, Hyderabad, or Chandni Chowk electing an individual MP, the Israeli electoral system requires some adjustment of understanding. There are no geographical parliamentary constituencies; the entire country functions as one national constituency.

All 120 members of the Knesset are elected through nationwide proportional representation. Voters choose a party list rather than an individual constituency candidate, and a list receiving at least 3.25 per cent of valid votes qualifies for representation. Seats are then allocated broadly according to each qualifying party’s share of the vote.

There are no reserved Arab seats. An Arab majority in Nazareth therefore does not elect “the MP for Nazareth” in the way voters in Hyderabad elect their Lok Sabha representative. Ballots cast in Nazareth enter the same national pool as those cast in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa or a West Bank settlement.

The terminology also requires care. “Arab Israelis”, “Palestinian citizens of Israel” and “Israeli Muslims” do not mean precisely the same thing. Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics estimated that at the end of 2025 there were 1.849 million Muslims, 18.6 per cent of all Israeli residents, while the broader Arab population also includes Christians and Druze.

Also, these citizens should not be confused with Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, who do not vote in Knesset elections. Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem have permanent residency rather than Israeli citizenship, though some have acquired citizenship.

After the 1948 war, roughly 1,60,000 Arabs remained inside what became Israel. By the end of 1967, Israeli statistics recorded roughly 2,90,000 Muslims. Today Muslims alone number nearly 1.85 million, which makes the comparatively modest number of seats held by Arab-majority parties one of the more intriguing features of Israeli electoral politics.
Where do votes go?

If roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population is Arab, elementary arithmetic might suggest something approaching 24 seats for Arabs in a 120-member parliament. Arab parties have never reached that figure; their best performance came in March 2020, when the Joint List won 15 seats after the Arab turnout climbed to nearly 65 per cent.
Israeli pollsters explain that Arab electoral participation has consistently lagged behind Jewish participation. In 2022, the Arab turnout stood at 53.2 per cent, far below the Jewish turnout.

Also, not every Arab citizen votes for an Arab-majority party. Some support Jewish-majority parties, while Druze voting patterns in particular have often differed from those of Muslim and Christian Arabs. The 3.25 per cent electoral threshold creates another hazard: a party falling below it receives no Knesset seats, so fragmentation can leave tens of thousands of votes without parliamentary representation.

The Arab electorate is itself far from homogeneous. In the 2022 election, the turnout in the north was 53.9 per cent. Hadash-Ta’al led there with 31.6 per cent, followed by Ra’am with 27.3 per cent, and Balad with 21.3 per cent. In northern Bedouin communities, by contrast, Ra’am captured nearly 69 per cent of the vote. For Arab politicians, this makes unity and turnout almost as important as their competition with Jewish parties.

The 2020 election demonstrated what greater unity and mobilisation could achieve. The Joint List won 15 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, the strongest result ever recorded by an Arab-majority electoral alliance.

The revived Joint List now brings together Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. Hadash comes from a communist and Arab-Jewish political tradition; Ta’al, long associated with Ahmad Tibi, combines Palestinian national demands with parliamentary pragmatism; while Balad represents a Palestinian nationalist current and advocates transforming Israel into a “state of all its citizens”.

Ra’am stands outside this alliance. Its roots lie in the southern branch of Israel’s Islamic Movement, but under Mansour Abbas it has pursued a markedly pragmatic course. Rather than resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict as a prerequisite for political participation, Abbas argues that Arab representatives have an immediate responsibility to address the problems confronting their own communities.

“I told the Arab citizens of the State of Israel that I want to address the economic, social, educational and housing problems in their communities,” he said, defending taking the plunge in electoral politics.

“We suffer from lots of crime. There are criminal organisations who take over our lives, our economy, even part of the local municipalities in Arab towns,” Abbas said. He rejected the notion that he had abandoned the Palestinian question. “I am concentrating on getting housing, education, infrastructure, employment and personal security while waiting for the larger conflict to be resolved,” he said.

Abbas tested this proposition in 2021 when Ra’am joined the coalition supporting the government headed first by Naftali Bennett and later Yair Lapid, an unprecedented step for an independent Arab party.

Supporters saw it as proof that Arab votes could finally be converted into budgets and bargaining power. But many within Palestinian society viewed the experiment differently, arguing that participation lent legitimacy to a political system that continued to privilege Jewish national identity while maintaining occupation beyond the Green Line.

Abbas has now taken the experiment further by placing Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish Zionist, former senior police officer and former Yesh Atid politician, second on Ra’am’s electoral slate. “There is a difficult history between Arabs and Jews in this country,” Segalovitz acknowledged while announcing the move, “but there is also a shared future.”

The symbolism is striking: a party with roots in an Islamist movement has placed a Jewish Zionist former police commander near the top of its electoral list. The Joint List offers a different route, with its leaders arguing that Arab political unity, rather than integration into Zionist-led governments, provides the best chance of maximising Palestinian electoral influence.
Outside both approaches is another view that questions whether parliamentary participation itself can fundamentally alter the relationship between Palestinian citizens and the Israeli state.

The lawyer Khaled Zbarqa has argued that Knesset politics risks reducing Palestinian political aspirations to budgets, legislation and tactical gains while leaving the deeper structure untouched, although he has also cautioned participants and boycotters against treating one another as enemies.

Former Balad chairman and Knesset member Mtanes Shehadeh comes from yet another tradition: participation in parliament, but as a means of asserting Palestinian national identity and demanding equal citizenship rather than accepting the ideological premises of Zionist parties.

These debates can sound theoretical until they are heard through the fatigue of ordinary voters. In Haifa’s predominantly Arab Wadi Nisnas neighbourhood, Walid Bolus captured that exhaustion during an earlier Israeli election when he asked: “Enough, how many times can we vote?”

The remark predates the present campaign, but the frustration it expressed remains measurable. An Israel Democracy Institute survey found the Arab public almost evenly divided over whether voting actually changes its situation: 48 per cent believed it did, while 52 per cent did not.

The question in 2026 is whether the possibility of greater political influence, combined with anxiety over crime and municipal conditions, can persuade some of those sceptical voters that participation is worthwhile.
Kingmakers nobody wants?

This is where Israeli electoral arithmetic becomes particularly curious. Arab parties can hold enough seats to matter when political blocs search for the 61 Knesset members required to form a government, while several major Jewish political forces remain unwilling to include them in a governing coalition.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief leading Yashar, has said Ra’am would not sit in a government headed by him. Netanyahu has turned the same issue into a campaign argument, warning Jewish voters against an opposition government dependent on Arab factions.

The result is a peculiar version of the kingmaker problem. Arab votes can become mathematically important in determining whether a bloc reaches 61 seats, while the parties receiving those votes may still be treated as politically unacceptable coalition partners. Their leverage therefore depends not simply on how many seats they win, but on whether Jewish-led parties are prepared to accept their support.

This is where the comparison with India becomes revealing, although the histories and constitutional structures are radically different. Indian Muslims have generally exercised electoral influence through national secular parties and regional formations rather than through a single national Muslim party.

First-past-the-post voting means that a minority concentrated in particular constituencies can become decisive without achieving proportional representation nationally. Israel produces almost the reverse phenomenon: its proportional system permits Palestinian citizens to create a visible parliamentary bloc, but coalition politics can impose a ceiling on what that bloc can achieve with its seats.

The present controversy in Israel has pushed that argument a stage further, from the question of how Palestinian citizens vote to whether their principal political formations can appear on the ballot at all.

The Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the two principal Arab lists. The human rights organisation Adalah argued that the decisions created a discriminatory standard by excluding the major Arab political formations while permitting far-right Jewish parties to compete.

For the past three years, Palestinian citizens of Israel have had to navigate a set of contradictions rarely captured by the familiar maps of the West Asia conflict. They have watched the destruction in Gaza with the anguish of people who share a Palestinian history and identity, while residents of their own towns have been killed by Hezbollah rockets and Iranian missiles.

Yet many have also felt increasingly constrained in expressing anger over what followed in Gaza. Alongside these larger conflicts are immediate concerns about violent crime, housing, employment, municipal resources, and the safety of their families.

When these citizens go to the polls on October 27, they will therefore be voting on much more than whether Benjamin Netanyahu remains Prime Minister or how Israel should deal with Gaza, Iran, and Lebanon. Their choices will also reflect an argument taking place within their own communities over whether parliamentary participation can improve everyday life; whether partnership with Jewish political parties offers a route to influence; and whether an Israeli political system built around the Jewish character of the state can accommodate Palestinian citizens as genuine partners in government.

That is what makes the Arab vote one of the most revealing contests within this election. Roughly one Israeli in five is Arab, but demographic weight has never translated automatically into an equivalent share of political power.

The test on October 27 will be whether greater participation and political organisation can narrow that gap, and whether the seats won by Arab parties can translate into a meaningful role in the negotiations that determine Israel’s next government.
Iftikhar Gilani is an Indian journalist based in Ankara.
